quiz.q: What kind of storage does the Mule Object Store provide?
quiz.explain: The Object Store is a Mule component for simple key-value storage, mainly for watermarks and temporary data like access tokens.

quiz.q: Why use an Object Store instead of a database for temporary data?
options: A database call is a costly external operation, better for permanent information
Databases are not allowed in Mule flows
quiz.explain: Database operations are costly and suited to permanent data; temporary data is cheaper in the object store.

quiz.q: A token is valid for 1 hour and your API gets 25 requests in that hour. With an Object Store, how many times do you call the token server?
quiz.explain: The first request generates and stores the token; requests 2–25 retrieve it — 1 call instead of 25.

quiz.q: A student asks why the token can't simply be kept in a variable. What is the answer?
options: Variables live only for that request's instance, so the next request can't see them
quiz.explain: When a request finishes its variables are killed; the object store is shared across requests.

quiz.q: The endpoint replies "invalid token" because the stored token expired. What did the class suggest?
options: Wrap the call in Try; in On Error Continue, Flow Reference the token sub-flow to regenerate and store it, then call again
Use On Error Propagate to return 401
quiz.explain: The same token sub-flow is reused through a flow reference, then the endpoint is called again.

quiz.q: Where is a transient Object Store kept, and what happens on restart?
quiz.explain: Transient is in memory: faster, but lost on restart, redeploy or crash. Persistent is on disk and kept.

quiz.q: Which storage type did the instructor choose for an access token?
options: Persistent, so it is never lost
Transient — faster, and losing it costs only one extra token call
quiz.explain: If the app restarts, the only cost is one extra token call, while every retrieve is faster from memory.

quiz.q: In the employee sync, what is the watermark?
options: The last processed point (e.g. the highest employee ID) so the next run selects only newer records
quiz.explain: "Where we stop — where we mark — is the watermark." The next query uses `employee ID > watermark`.

quiz.q: The watermark is 104 after 25 Jan, and employees 105–108 are added. What does the 26 Jan run do?
quiz.explain: The query is dynamic — it uses the stored value, then the max of the new IDs is stored.

quiz.q: The watermark is kept in a transient store and the app restarts at 10 pm. What happens on the next run?
options: It continues from the last ID
It falls back to the default (99), reprocesses everything and creates duplicates / Salesforce errors
It reads the watermark from Salesforce automatically
quiz.explain: That's why watermarks need persistent storage — there's no system to "get it again".

quiz.q: Which Mule feature uses an object store in the background?
quiz.explain: Cache is also temporary storage, and its data is stored in an object store underneath.

cards.back: A Mule component for simple **key-value** storage — mainly for watermarks and temporary data like access tokens. A generic concept, not MuleSoft-specific.

cards.front: What is the Object Store used for?
cards.back: Temporary or synchronization data — typically **access tokens** and **watermarks** — without the cost of a database call.

cards.front: Why not store temporary data in a database?
cards.back: A database call is a costly external operation, right for permanent information. The object store is cheaper for temporary data.

cards.front: Why not store the token in a variable?
cards.back: Variables live only for one request; the next request can't see them. The object store is shared across requests.

cards.front: Access token flow with an Object Store
cards.back: Retrieve → nothing there → generate token → Store → call API. Later requests: Retrieve → found → call API directly.

cards.front: How do you handle an expired token?
cards.back: Wrap the call in Try; on "invalid token", On Error Continue calls the token sub-flow (Flow Reference) to regenerate and store it, then retries.
Transient = memory, faster, lost on restart. Persistent = disk, a bit slower, kept after restart/redeploy/crash.

cards.front: Transient or persistent for an access token?
cards.back: **Transient** — faster, and losing it costs only one more token call.

cards.front: Transient or persistent for a watermark?
cards.back: **Persistent** — losing it after a restart would reprocess everything and create duplicates.
Remembering where the last run stopped (e.g. max employee ID) so the next run selects only newer records: `where id > :watermark`, then store the new max.
Scheduler → Object Store **Retrieve** (default value) → DB Select `> watermark` → Salesforce Create → Object Store **Store** the max ID.

cards.front: Why is a default value needed on the first run?
cards.back: Nothing is stored yet, so Retrieve returns the default (e.g. 99) and the query picks up all employees.

cards.front: Why not insert all employees every run?
cards.back: The employee ID is unique, so inserting the same employee twice errors. Send everything the first time, then only new ones.
Cache (and HTTP caching) stores its data in an object store in the background.
The name under which data is stored / the stored data — e.g. a whole address saved as the value under one key.
The server that issues access tokens for an OAuth/JWT-protected API.
